question: From which country is the legislative procedure in the Indian Constitution taken from ?
solution:
The correct answer is __**United Kingdom**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The legislative procedure in the Indian Constitution is primarily derived from the **United Kingdom**, reflecting the parliamentary system of governance.
 
• The Indian parliamentary system incorporates the concept of a **bicameral legislature**, consisting of the Lok Sabha (House of the People) and the Rajya Sabha (Council of States), similar to the UK’s House of Commons and House of Lords.
 
• The principle of collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers to the Lok Sabha is also inspired by the British system.
 
• The role of the Speaker, the opposition, and the parliamentary debate procedures in India are closely modeled after the UK Parliament.
 
• While the legislative framework draws from the UK, it has been tailored to suit India’s federal structure and diverse population.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Bicameral Legislature:** A legislative system with two houses, ensuring checks and balances. In India, it consists of the Lok Sabha (lower house) and Rajya Sabha (upper house).
 
• **Parliamentary System:** India follows a parliamentary system where the executive (Council of Ministers) is accountable to the legislature (Parliament).
 
• **Collective Responsibility:** A concept where the entire Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha, ensuring accountability in governance.
 
• **Role of the Speaker:** The Speaker of the Lok Sabha, akin to the Speaker of the House of Commons in the UK, maintains order and decorum during debates.
 
• **Federal Adaptation:** While inspired by the UK, the Indian system integrates features like a written constitution and a federal structure, which are absent in the UK's unitary system.
